name: Permissioned Blockchain
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Permissioned Blockchains: Not Everyone Gets to Play
lesson.summary: A permissioned blockchain restricts who may validate transactions or write to the ledger, replacing open participation with an explicit authorization gate.
lesson.body:
A permissioned blockchain is a network where participation, particularly the ability to validate transactions and add new blocks, requires explicit approval from a controlling entity or a defined set of entities. Before a computer can act as a node on the network, someone with authority over the system has to grant it that role. This stands in direct contrast to the open, anyone-can-join model most people associate with blockchain in general, and it is worth remembering that the blockchain data structure itself, a chain of cryptographically linked blocks, says nothing about who is allowed to add to it. That question is answered separately, by the network's access rules.

This is where authorization, a concept that normally governs what an already identified party is allowed to do within a system, gets applied at the most fundamental level a blockchain has: participation itself. In a typical application, authorization decides whether a logged in user can view a file or approve a payment. In a permissioned blockchain, the same idea decides whether a given organization's server is allowed to run as a validating node at all. Identity comes first, usually verified through some off chain process, and only afterward is that identity authorized for specific roles such as submitting transactions, validating blocks, or reading ledger contents.

Organizations choose this model for reasons that make sense once you consider who is actually running the network. Known, accountable participants make regulatory compliance far easier, since regulators can point to a specific, identified organization responsible for a validating node rather than an anonymous global pool of miners. Known participants also make it practical to design consensus that does not require the expensive computational competition of open networks. Because validators are already trusted to some degree by virtue of being vetted and authorized, permissioned networks can use faster, less resource intensive consensus protocols instead of proof of work, since the goal shifts from stopping anonymous attackers to catching honest mistakes or the rare misbehaving insider.

A concrete example helps make this less abstract. Imagine a group of regulated banks that want a shared ledger for settling trades among themselves. They have no interest in letting anonymous members of the public run validating nodes on a system that touches real interbank settlement, both for regulatory reasons and because the trust problem they are solving is different: it is not about trusting strangers, it is about efficiently synchronizing records among institutions that already have legal relationships and obligations to each other.

The trade off is real, and it is the central tension this chapter sets up for the rest of the unit. By gatekeeping participation, a permissioned blockchain gives up the censorship resistance and open entry that give permissionless networks like Bitcoin much of their appeal, since it reintroduces exactly the kind of trusted gatekeeper that decentralized blockchains are often marketed as eliminating. Whether that trade off is worth it depends entirely on what problem the network is actually trying to solve, a question the following chapters on permissionless, private, and consortium blockchains will keep returning to.
